title: Why I'm Learning LLMs as a Systems Programmer
excerpt: I write Rust and study ray tracers. So why am I now deep in transformer architecture papers? Here's my honest take on where systems skills meet the AI wave.
content:
## An Unlikely Turn

My natural habitat is low-level code — memory allocators, rendering pipelines, shader programs. The kind of work where you can reason about every CPU cycle. So why, in 2025, did I start reading Andrej Karpathy's lectures on LLMs at 11pm?

Simple: I couldn't ignore it anymore.

## The Systems Angle

Here's what I didn't expect: understanding LLMs well requires exactly the skills I've been building for years.

**Linear algebra** — transformers are essentially massive matrix multiplications. The attention mechanism is a learned weighted average across a sequence. You can't understand why things like quantization work without understanding the geometry.

**Memory and compute tradeoffs** — training and inference optimization is deeply systems work. Techniques like FlashAttention aren't magic; they're cache-aware algorithm design. Fused kernels, memory-efficient attention, KV caching — this is the GPU programming mindset applied to ML.

**Concurrency** — distributed training across hundreds of GPUs requires tensor parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and careful synchronization. This is networking and distributed systems, just at ML scale.

## What I'm Actually Studying

**Transformer architecture** — I started with Karpathy's *makemore* series before building a minimal GPT implementation. Understanding attention from first principles (not just the API) matters.

**Fine-tuning and PEFT** — LoRA and QLoRA let you adapt large models with remarkably small compute. The math behind why low-rank adaptations work connects nicely to SVD and linear algebra.

**Inference optimization** — speculative decoding, quantization, and continuous batching. This is where my systems background directly applies.

## The Honest Part

I'm not trying to become a researcher. I'm not going to out-deep-learn teams at OpenAI. But I am a developer who wants to *build things with LLMs well* — and that means understanding the layer below the API.

When I know how attention works, I write better prompts. When I understand context windows and tokenization, I design better retrieval pipelines. When I've seen the training dynamics, I'm less likely to be fooled by benchmarks.

## What's Next

I'm working toward building a small RAG-based system that combines my interest in structured data and language models. The goal isn't a product — it's to close the loop between reading papers and shipping something real.

If you're a systems programmer wondering whether to learn this: the answer is yes. The implementation details are more familiar than you think.
